L9@P0: Abstract. In this article, we generalize the works of Pan et al. (Eurocrypt’21) and Porter et al. (ArXiv’21) and provide a simple condition
L10@P0: under which an ideal lattice defines an easy instance of the shortest vector problem. Namely, we show that the more automorphisms stabilize
L11@P0: the ideal, the easier it is to find a short vector in it. This observation
L12@P0: was already made for prime ideals in Galois fields, and we generalize it
L13@P0: to any ideal (whose prime factors are not ramified) of any number field.
L14@P0: We then provide a cryptographic application of this result by showing
L15@P0: that particular instances of the partial Vandermonde knapsack problem,
L16@P0: also known as partial Fourier recovery problem, can be solved classically
L17@P0: in polynomial time. As a proof of concept, we implemented our attack
L18@P0: and managed to solve those particular instances for concrete parameter
L19@P0: settings proposed in the literature. For random instances, we can halve
L20@P0: the lattice dimension with non-negligible probability.
L21@P0: 1 Introduction
L22@P0: Euclidean lattices are mathematical objects that play an important role in many
L23@P0: areas of mathematics and computer science. There are several computational
L24@P0: problems related to lattices that are proven to be NP-hard, for instance, the
L25@P0: problem of finding a shortest vector (SVP) or a set of shortest independent
L26@P0: vectors (SIVP) in a given lattice. A standard relaxation consists in solving them
L27@P0: only up to some approximation factor γ ≥ 1, denoted γ-S(I)VP. It is commonly
L28@P0: conjectured that the problems remain hard to solve for approximation factors
L29@P0: that are polynomial in the lattice rank. Their presumed intractability provides a
L30@P0: fundamental starting point for the construction of provably secure cryptographic
L31@P0: schemes, shown in the seminal works of Ajtai [Ajt96] and Regev [Reg05].

In order to improve efficiency, problems
L33@P1: on structured lattices have been introduced, e.g., [Mic02,LM06,PR06,SSTX09,
L34@P1: LPR10, LS15]. The most popular setting is to consider OK-modules of rank r,
L35@P1: where OK is the ring of integers of some number field K of degree d. By applying the d different field embeddings from K to C, any OK-module of rank r
L36@P1: is mapped to a lattice of rank d · r. Those lattices inherit the module structure
L37@P1: (i.e., closed with respect to scalar multiplication by ring elements) and are called
L38@P1: module lattices. If the module rank equals 1, they are called ideal lattices.
L39@P1: Many structured lattice assumptions, such as Ring-LWE [SSTX09,LPR10],
L40@P1: NTRU [HPS98] or Module-LWE [LS15] can be solved with an SVP solver in
L41@P1: module lattices of small rank (≥ 2). This motivates the study of the hardness
L42@P1: of SVP in module lattices. To start tackling this problem, many algorithms
L43@P1: have focused on the special case of solving SVP in rank-1 modules, that is in
L44@P1: ideals. This restricted problem is denoted by Id-SVP. While solving Id-SVP
L45@P1: is not known to break any of the three lattice assumptions mentioned above,
L46@P1: studying this (potentially easier) problem can be seen as a first step to better
L47@P1: understand the hardness behind algebraically structured lattices. Another motivation for studying Id-SVP comes from the fact that the first hardness result
L48@P1: for Ring-LWE was a reduction from worst-case Id-SVP [SSTX09,LPR10]. This
L49@P1: reduction only provides a lower bound on the hardness of Ring-LWE, and we
L50@P1: have today a stronger reduction, from worst-case SVP in modules of rank ≥ 2,
L51@P1: for some more restricted regime of parameters of Ring-LWE [AD17]. Still, even if
L52@P1: an efficient algorithm for Id-SVP would not have a direct impact on the security
L53@P1: of Ring-LWE, it would make the reduction from Id-SVP vacuous, and hence let
L54@P1: some interesting regime of Ring-LWE without lower bound security guarantees.
